tests.q: The what-if "profit if discounts were capped at 20%" is best described as:

tests.q: State is shown as "Abc" and will not draw a map. What do you do?

tests.q: Which chart best shows how a single order-value variable is distributed?
tests.h: Histograms show distributions; create bins first.

tests.lesson: Charts in Tableau: From Bar and Line to Maps, Dual Axis, Histograms and Pareto
tests.q: How do you get Profit as a line on top of Sales bars with its own scale?

tests.h: Dual axis gives two independent axes and separate mark types.

tests.q: Which is the right way to show 13 sub-categories as a part-to-whole?
tests.h: Pies stop being readable beyond about five slices.

tests.q: You want each year as its own line to compare seasonality. What goes on Columns?

tests.q: What does the Pareto line show?
o: The running total of sales as a percent of the grand total
tests.h: Running total + percent of total secondary calculation.

tests.q: When should you synchronise a dual axis?
o: When both measures share the same unit and scale makes sense
When one is in ₹ and the other in %

tests.lesson: Calculations in Tableau: Calculated Fields, Table Calculations and LOD Expressions
tests.q: Which formula gives the correct profit margin for a category?
tests.h: Divide the totals; do not average row ratios.

tests.q: You need "Top 10 products within the selected region". What must you do?
o: Add the Region filter to context

tests.q: A parameter on its own does nothing. Why?
o: It must be referenced by a calculation, filter or reference line
It must be added to context
It only works on Tableau Server
tests.h: Parameters are inputs that something must use.

tests.lesson: Filters, Parameters, Sets, Groups and Hierarchies in Tableau
tests.q: Which filter applies to every sheet using the data source and is good for row-level restrictions?
tests.h: Data source filters run near the start for all sheets.

tests.lesson: Filters, Parameters, Sets, Groups and Hierarchies in Tableau
tests.q: Which set type keeps the 10 largest customers by sales, updating as data changes?

o: A CASE on a string parameter returning SUM([Sales]), SUM([Profit]) or SUM([Quantity])
tests.h: The parameter value chooses the branch.

o: The join repeated each target once per sales line

tests.h: Unions stack rows of same-shaped tables.

o: When two sources cannot be joined in one data source and you link them on a common dimension in a sheet
tests.h: Blends combine separate sources after aggregation.

tests.q: Your Excel sheet has a title row and merged headers. What helps first?
tests.h: Data Interpreter detects the real table.

tests.q: Which is TRUE about extracts?
o: They are fast compressed snapshots that need refreshing
They only work on Tableau Server
tests.h: Schedule full or incremental refreshes.

tests.lesson: Data Modelling in Tableau: Relationships, Joins, Unions, Blending, Extracts and Tableau Prep
tests.q: Where do relationships live?
tests.h: Double-click a logical table to see its physical joins.

tests.q: Which action makes clicking a state on a map filter every other chart?
o: A filter action (or Use as Filter)
tests.h: Filter actions pass the selected values to target sheets.

tests.q: Which feature expands a category into its sub-categories in place when clicked?
o: A set action with a calculation that switches between Category and Sub-Category
tests.h: Change Set Values drives the drill-in pattern.

tests.lesson: Dashboards, Actions, Stories and Publishing in Tableau (Capstone)
tests.q: Where should the KPI cards usually go?
o: Across the top-left of the dashboard
tests.h: Readers start top-left (Z-pattern).

tests.lesson: Dashboards, Actions, Stories and Publishing in Tableau (Capstone)
tests.q: What is a Story in Tableau?
o: A sequence of captioned story points showing sheets or dashboards
tests.h: Stories present an analysis step by step.

tests.lesson: Dashboards, Actions, Stories and Publishing in Tableau (Capstone)
tests.q: Which is NOT available on Tableau Public?
o: Keeping your workbook private on the server
tests.h: Everything saved to Tableau Public is public.

tests.q: How do you make one Region filter apply to all sheets on a dashboard?
o: Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source (or Selected Worksheets)
Duplicate the filter on every sheet
tests.h: One filter can drive many sheets.

tests.lesson: Figma Complete Tutorial: Interface, Auto Layout, Components, Variables, Prototypes, Dev Mode and Figma AI

o: Stacks children with a set direction, gap and padding so the frame resizes with its content
tests.h: It works like CSS flexbox.

tests.q: You need Primary/Secondary buttons in three sizes and three states. What should you build?
o: One component set with variant properties Type, Size and State
tests.h: Variants keep related components in one set.

tests.q: Which feature lets one frame switch between Light and Dark colours?

tests.h: 3:1 applies to large text.

tests.h: Dev Mode is built for handoff.

It runs once with all rows

tests.h: $json is the current item's data.

tests.h: You can also import a cURL command into it.

tests.q: What is the main reason teams self-host n8n?
o: Data stays on their own servers and code/npm packages are allowed
tests.h: Cloud is easier; self-hosting gives control.

o: A chat model, memory, tools and an optional output parser

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: A team ships 12 features but checkout completion barely moves. Which statement is most accurate?
o: They did great work because output was high.
They produced high output but low outcome.
Checkout completion is not a valid metric.
tests.h: Output counts what was built; outcome measures the change in user or business results. High output with flat outcome is the feature-factory pattern.

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: In Scrum, how long can a sprint be?
tests.h: The Scrum Guide sets sprints at one month or less; two weeks is a common choice, not a rule.

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: Which is NOT strong evidence of product–market fit?
o: Many users saying they'd be very disappointed to lose the product
tests.h: Market size says there could be demand; fit requires evidence that real customers keep using and valuing the product.

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: Which risk does a usability test mainly reduce?
tests.h: Usability tests check whether users can figure out how to use the solution. Value, feasibility and viability need other evidence.

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: A sales lead asks for a PDF export. What should the PM do first?
o: Ask what the customer does with it and what outcome they need
tests.h: Requests are solutions; the underlying job determines the best option and the cost-benefit.

tests.lesson: Module 1
tests.q: Which model most strongly encourages empowered teams?
tests.h: Empowered teams are given problems to solve and measurable outcomes, not a list of solutions.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: Which best describes a roadmap?
o: A guarantee of dates for specific features
A communicated plan of outcomes and likely work, derived from strategy
A list of all customer requests
tests.h: A roadmap communicates priorities and direction over time; it is evolving and follows strategy.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: In the Ansoff matrix, selling the current product to a new market is…
tests.h: Existing product + new market = market development.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: Which sizing approach is preferred?
o: Bottom-up: users × frequency × price, with a range
The biggest number you can cite
tests.h: Bottom-up estimates expose assumptions you can test. Arbitrary percentages of a giant market are not evidence.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: A strong network effect exists when…
o: Many people have downloaded the app
Each additional user makes the product more valuable for existing users, enough to resist rivals
The product is popular on social media
tests.h: Network effects mean marginal users add value to others; they are often local and can be weakened by multi-homing.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: Which is a well-formed key result?
o: Increase checkout completion from 70% to 76% for new users this quarter, complaints ≤ 1.3%
tests.h: A key result has a baseline, target, population, time frame and often a guardrail.

tests.lesson: Module 2
tests.q: Which is a substitute rather than a direct competitor?
o: Cooking at home instead of ordering
A copy-cat app with same features
tests.h: Substitutes meet the same need (a meal) in a different way and compete for the same outcome, time or budget.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: Which is an example of secondary quantitative research?
o: A survey you design and send
A published market report with spending figures
tests.h: Secondary research uses existing information; quantitative means numeric evidence. A published report fits both.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: Which interview question is best?
o: Would you use an app that shows fees early?
Tell me about the last time the total changed at checkout.
tests.h: It asks about a specific past experience, is neutral and invites a story.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: In the four forces of switching, 'anxiety' refers to…
o: Worries about trying the new solution
tests.h: Push and pull move people toward switching; anxiety and habit hold them back.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: 6 of 8 interviewees mention the fee surprise. How should you report it?
o: 6 of 8 interviewed participants mentioned it; frequency in the population is unknown
Ignore it; the sample is too small
tests.h: Small qualitative samples reveal themes, not population percentages.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: On an assumption map, which should you test first?
tests.h: Assumptions that would sink the idea and that you know little about carry the most risk per test.

tests.lesson: Module 3
tests.q: A guesstimate gives 480k/day top-down and 495k/day bottom-up. The right conclusion is…
o: Confidence is higher but both depend on assumptions; give a range
tests.h: Agreement of independent methods raises confidence, but communicate a range and the key assumptions.

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: RICE for Reach 20,000, Impact 1, Confidence 80%, Effort 2 equals…

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: In RICE, increasing Effort…
tests.h: Effort is the denominator, so more effort lowers the score.

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: A regulatory deadline item should usually be…
o: Scored with RICE like everything else
Taken off the top as mandatory work
Dropped if its score is low
tests.h: Mandatory legal, security or contractual work is scheduled regardless of score.

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: Which describes a Kano 'must-be' feature?
o: Its absence dissatisfies but presence is just expected
More of it always raises satisfaction
tests.h: Must-be features are expected basics: absent = dissatisfied; present = neutral.

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: WSJF is computed as…
tests.h: Weighted Shortest Job First divides Cost of Delay by job size.

tests.lesson: Module 4
tests.q: An MVP is best described as…
o: The cheapest version of the full product
The smallest useful version or experiment to learn about a key assumption
tests.h: MVPs are defined by what they let you learn; they may be non-public and need not be a prototype.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: Which statement correctly contrasts UX and UI?
o: UI is the whole experience; UX is the buttons.
UX is the whole experience; UI is the interface people see and use.
UX applies only to mobile apps.
tests.h: UX covers the full experience of achieving a goal, including usability, trust and failure handling; UI is the visual and interactive layer.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: Hick's law says decision time…
o: Increases with the number and complexity of choices
tests.h: More (and more complex) choices take longer to process; group and prioritise options.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: Fitts's law implies a primary mobile button should be…
o: Small and far from the thumb
tests.h: Time to reach a target falls as it gets closer and larger.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: Normal body text needs at least what contrast ratio for WCAG AA?
tests.h: WCAG 2.2 AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI components.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: Why run several small usability rounds rather than one large one?
o: It is cheaper per participant only
Each round finds most problems, you fix them, then retest to find the next layer
tests.h: Small samples find most usability problems; iterating compounds the benefit.

tests.lesson: Module 5
tests.q: A good error message…
o: Explains what happened and how to recover, in plain language
tests.h: Heuristic 9: help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors.

tests.lesson: Module 6
tests.q: The Pyramid Principle recommends…
o: Building up to the conclusion at the end
Starting with the answer, then grouped supporting arguments
tests.h: Lead with the governing thought, then MECE support and evidence.

tests.lesson: Module 6
tests.q: In DACI, who makes the final decision?
tests.h: The Approver decides; the Driver runs the process.

tests.lesson: Module 6
tests.q: Which is a well-formed acceptance criterion?
o: Given an eligible address, when the cart opens, then show the estimated total.
tests.h: Acceptance criteria are specific and testable, often Given/When/Then.

tests.lesson: Module 6
tests.q: Focusing on interests rather than positions means…
o: Understanding the need behind a demand to find better options
tests.h: Interests reveal options that satisfy the underlying need.

tests.lesson: Module 6
tests.q: Story points are best described as…
o: Relative effort estimates for a team's planning
tests.h: Story points are team-relative planning estimates, not productivity scores.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: A funnel has 800 of 1,000 visitors completing a step. What are step conversion and drop-off?
tests.h: Step conversion = 800 ÷ 1,000 = 80%; drop-off = 1 − 0.80 = 20%.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: AOV is best defined as…
o: Total order value ÷ number of orders
tests.h: AOV = total order value ÷ number of orders for the same period and definition. It says nothing by itself about profit.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: A test gives p = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
o: There is a 97% chance the variant is better.
If there were truly no difference, results this extreme would occur about 3% of the time.
The result will replicate 97% of the time.
tests.h: A p-value is a probability about the data under the null hypothesis. It is not the probability the variant works and says nothing about effect size.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: Which change makes the required sample size per arm increase the most?
tests.h: Sample size scales roughly with 1/(effect size)², so halving the MDE roughly quadruples the sample.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: LTV (simple) = ₹120 ÷ 0.05 is ₹2,400. If churn rises to 8%, LTV becomes…
tests.h: 120 ÷ 0.08 = ₹1,500. LTV is very sensitive to churn.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: In Simpson's paradox, the overall result is reversed relative to every segment because of…
tests.h: When the variant gets a different mix of high- and low-converting segments, the aggregate can mislead; proper randomisation and segmenting fix it.

tests.lesson: Module 7
tests.q: Which should NOT be sent as an analytics event property?
tests.h: Card details (and typically emails and phone numbers) must never go into analytics tools.

tests.lesson: Module 8
tests.q: Users send 4 invites each and 5% convert. What is K?
tests.h: K = invites per user × conversion = 4 × 0.05 = 0.2.

tests.lesson: Module 8
tests.q: NRR above 100% means…
o: Revenue from existing customers grew after expansion, contraction and churn
tests.h: NRR measures revenue from the starting cohort including expansion, contraction and churn; it excludes new customers.

tests.lesson: Module 8
tests.q: Which is involuntary churn?
o: Card expires and renewal payment fails
tests.h: Involuntary churn comes from payment failures rather than a choice to leave.

tests.lesson: Module 8
tests.q: A staged rollout primarily helps you…
o: Limit blast radius and check guardrails before full exposure
tests.h: Gradual exposure with gates and a kill switch limits damage from unexpected problems.

tests.lesson: Module 8
tests.q: In PLG, the best moment for an upgrade prompt is…
o: When the user hits a limit after getting real value
tests.h: Upgrade prompts convert best at moments of demonstrated value or need.

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: A user is logged in but tries to view another user's order and gets blocked. Which status code fits?
tests.h: 403 Forbidden: authenticated but not authorised. (Some APIs return 404 to avoid revealing existence.)

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: Why use an idempotency key on payment requests?
o: So retries don't create duplicate charges
tests.h: Idempotency ensures repeating the same request has the same effect as doing it once.

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: Three services at 99.9% availability in series give roughly…

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: Which metric best reflects the slow experiences some users have?
tests.h: Tail percentiles capture the worst experiences that averages hide.

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: OAuth 2.0 is primarily for…
tests.h: OAuth lets an app access resources on a user's behalf without their password; OIDC adds identity.

tests.lesson: Module 9
tests.q: Feature flags are useful because they…
o: Let you turn features on/off or roll out gradually without redeploying
tests.h: Flags enable staged rollouts, experiments and kill switches.

tests.lesson: Module 10
tests.q: Which statement about RAG is correct?
o: RAG retrains the model on your documents
RAG retrieves relevant content at answer time and adds it to the model's context
tests.h: RAG is retrieval at question time; it doesn't retrain the model, and retrieval can be keyword, semantic or hybrid.

tests.lesson: Module 10
tests.q: Two embeddings have cosine similarity 0.98. This means…
o: They are very similar in the model's representation
One is a copy of the other
tests.h: High cosine similarity indicates closeness in embedding space, not truth or identical wording.

tests.lesson: Module 10
tests.q: When is fine-tuning most appropriate?
o: To add knowledge that changes daily
To get consistent behaviour/format on a stable task with many good examples
tests.h: Fine-tuning shapes behaviour; it's poor for fresh knowledge and doesn't eliminate hallucinations.

tests.lesson: Module 10

pm.q: What is your favourite product and why?
pm.a: “Google Maps for commuting. My job is ‘get to work on time with least stress.’ It works because (1) live traffic turns uncertainty into an ETA I trust, (2) it re-routes proactively, (3) it combines modes. A weakness for me: on crowded metro lines it doesn't tell me how full trains are, so I can't choose a less crowded one. I'd test showing crowding levels from anonymised, aggregated data, measuring route-choice changes and satisfaction, with privacy as a guardrail.”

pm.q: What makes a product great?
pm.a: “A great product reliably helps a specific user make progress on an important job, with as little effort and risk as possible, in a way the business can sustain. Signals: users return without being pushed (retention curves flatten), they recommend it, and the economics improve with scale. Example: a payments flow that just works at checkout — invisible reliability is a feature.”

pm.q: Critique the onboarding of an app you used recently.
pm.a: “A budgeting app asked for bank linking, notifications and goals before showing anything useful. Heuristic: visibility and user control — I had no idea what value I'd get. Biggest fix: show a sample dashboard immediately and ask for bank linking in context when I tap ‘see my spending’. Metric: activation (first budget created within 3 days); guardrails: permission grant rate, privacy complaints.”

pm.q: Which product do you think is badly designed, and how would you fix it?
pm.a: “Many parking-payment apps: you must register, add a card and find a zone code while standing in the street. Constraint: municipalities require identification and payment records. Fix: a QR on the meter that opens a lightweight web flow with wallet payment, with optional account creation later. Trade-off: less data capture; mitigate with optional emailed receipts.”

pm.q: How would you improve YouTube Shorts?
pm.a: “I'd focus on new viewers whose first Shorts feel irrelevant — they leave before personalisation kicks in. Ideas: a lightweight topic picker after the first few swipes; a ‘not interested’ that visibly teaches the feed; separation of short vs long results in search. I'd A/B the topic picker; primary: day-7 return rate of new viewers; guardrails: session-satisfaction surveys and time-spent spikes among younger users.”

pm.q: Should Netflix let users stop a title from leaving the catalogue?
pm.a: “The need is real — losing a show mid-watch is frustrating — but licences expire contractually, so a ‘keep’ button is usually infeasible. Better: warn earlier (‘leaving in 14 days’), a ‘finish before it leaves’ row, and use the count of mid-watch members as a signal in licence negotiations.”

pm.q: What product would you build for elderly users to manage medicines?
pm.a: “Start with a caregiver-set schedule and a very simple ‘taken’ confirmation (large button, voice option); missed-dose alerts to a caregiver after a grace period; pharmacy refill reminders. Avoid medical advice; partner with pharmacists for dose data. Metrics: doses confirmed on time; caregiver alerts resolved. Guardrails: false alarms, privacy consent.”

pm.q: What is a product you think will fail, and why?
pm.a: “I'd question standalone AI gadgets that duplicate phone capabilities: the job (quick answers) is already served by phones; the device adds cost and charging burden; switching costs favour phones. It could succeed only if it serves a job phones do badly — hands-free contexts or accessibility. I'd watch day-30 retention and daily use versus phone usage.”

pm.q: Design a search engine for children under 14.
pm.a: “Focus on 8–12-year-olds doing homework. Needs: readable results, trustworthy sources, no unsuitable content, parents' reassurance. Design: curated educational sources first, reading-level summaries, image search with strict filtering, ‘ask a grown-up’ prompts for sensitive topics, a parent dashboard with privacy-preserving summaries. Filtering is imperfect — don't promise complete safety; add a report button; no personalised ads. Metrics: task success (found an answer); parent trust score; guardrail: unsafe-content reports.”

pm.q: Help a professional regain control of an overflowing inbox after a holiday.
pm.a: “Job: find what's urgent and relevant without reading everything. Design: a ‘Catch-up’ view grouped by people I work with, deadlines and mentions; AI thread summaries with links to originals; bulk actions with preview and undo. Risks: misclassifying an important email, wrongly auto-archiving, exposing confidential data to AI — keep human review for bulk actions, test accuracy, respect permissions. Metric: time to clear important items; guardrail: ‘missed important email’ reports.”

pm.q: Design a feature to reduce food-delivery checkout abandonment.
pm.a: “First confirm where users drop — say, the payment step. If research shows fee surprise, show an estimated total in the cart with ‘est.’ labels, refresh on address change, and an honest ‘Estimate unavailable’ fallback if the fee service fails. A/B test with checkout completion as primary; complaints and payment errors as guardrails.” *(See Modules 5 and 7.)*

pm.q: Design a dating feature for a large social network.
pm.a: “Segment by intention (serious vs casual). Core: opt-in profile separate from the main profile, verified identity, mutual-interest reveal, events-based matching. Safety: consent, harassment reporting, location fuzzing, age verification, no exposure of private conversations. Monetisation: freemium features that don't compromise safety (no paying to message strangers). Metric: mutual matches that lead to conversations; guardrails: reports per 1,000 users, blocks.”

pm.q: Design an ATM for the visually impaired.
pm.a: “Audio guidance via a headphone jack, a tactile keypad with raised markers, phone-based pre-staging (set the withdrawal in the app, then tap card/phone), screen blanking for privacy, consistent layouts and generous timeouts. Test with visually impaired users; measure task success and time; guardrail: fraud and shoulder-surfing incidents.”

pm.q: Design a parking app for a busy city.
pm.a: “Users: daily commuters vs occasional visitors. Jobs: find a spot quickly, pay easily, avoid fines. Features: live availability (sensors/partner garages), reserve and pay, extend remotely, reminders before expiry. Metrics: time to park, successful reservations, fine reduction (self-reported). Risks: inaccurate availability → show confidence levels.”

pm.q: Design a product to help small restaurants reduce food waste.
pm.a: “Job: prepare and order the right quantities. Start with a simple demand forecast from past sales + weather + local events, giving suggested prep quantities; later add a marketplace for end-of-day surplus. Low integration first (POS export/CSV). Metrics: waste % by weight, margin; guardrail: stock-outs.”

pm.q: Design a feature to increase channel-creation quality in a team-chat tool.
pm.a: “Suggest similar existing channels when someone types a new channel name; offer naming templates and pre-filled purposes; improve directory search. Primary metric: duplicate-channel rate; secondary: channel-message share. Randomise by workspace to avoid contamination.” *(See Case 7 and Project 3.)*

pm.q: Design an emergency feature for a ride-hailing app.
pm.a: “Users: rider, driver, emergency contacts, safety operations. Features: an SOS button that shares live location with emergency services/contacts per local rules, trip sharing, unusual-stop detection with a check-in prompt, and a safety centre. Design for false positives without delaying urgent calls; offline/poor-network fallback (SMS). Metrics: time to response, check-in resolution; guardrails: false alarms, privacy.”

pm.q: Should a food-delivery company launch grocery delivery?
pm.a: “It's product development in an existing market (Ansoff). Assets: customer base, courier network, app. Need: fast top-ups for urban households. Economics differ: lower AOV and margin, inventory and dark stores. I'd pilot in two dense neighbourhoods with a limited assortment, measure repeat rate, contribution per order and cannibalisation of food orders, and scale only if contribution turns positive within ~6 months.”

pm.q: How should a travel marketplace respond to a sudden collapse in travel (e.g., a pandemic)?
pm.a: “Focus on demand that still exists — nearby getaways and long stays for remote workers; adapt search to flexible destinations and monthly stays; strengthen trust with cleaning standards and flexible cancellation; support hosts with clear refund rules. Measure booking recovery by segment, host retention and refund disputes.”

pm.q: How would you enter a new country with a fintech product?
pm.a: “Scan regulation, payments infrastructure and trust (PESTLE); choose a beachhead segment; partner with a licensed local bank first rather than seeking a licence; localise language, KYC documents and payment methods; pilot in one city. Key risks: regulatory timelines and new fraud patterns. Metrics: activation, fraud rate, CAC payback.”

pm.q: A competitor launched a cheaper version of our product. What do you do?
pm.a: “Don't react instantly. Check churn and win/loss by segment, interview switchers, and see whether price or features drive it. Options: hold price and sharpen value messaging; launch a lighter tier for price-sensitive users; bundle; raise switching value ethically. Choose based on margin impact and which segment matters strategically.”

pm.q: Should a music-streaming service expand into podcasts or audiobooks?
pm.a: “Frame it as expanding from ‘music’ to ‘audio companionship’. Benefits: more listening time, differentiation, ad inventory. Costs: content and rights, discovery complexity. Strategy: invest in discovery and creator tools rather than only exclusives. Measure incremental listening time and retention, not catalogue size.”

pm.q: Build, buy or partner for identity verification?
pm.a: “Buy or partner: identity verification is regulated and commodity-like, and speed matters. Keep control of the onboarding UX and data handling, check vendor compliance and uptime, build an abstraction layer to switch vendors, and revisit building only if scale economics or differentiation justify it.”

pm.q: What is the moat for a ride-hailing company?
pm.a: “Local network effects (density cuts wait times), brand trust and safety record, data for pricing and ETAs, and driver relationships. Weaknesses: riders and drivers multi-home, and regulation. So the moat is local and must be continuously defended with reliability and driver economics.”

pm.q: How would you set a 3-year vision and strategy for a B2B SaaS product?
pm.a: “Vision: the customer future (e.g., ‘every team closes the loop on decisions’). Strategy: win a beachhead, then adjacent segments; three product pillars; integrations as a platform; GTM from PLG to sales-assist; pricing evolution; an NSM with guardrails; explicit ‘won't do’ list. Validate yearly with retention, NRR and win/loss.”

pm.q: Your launch is slipping by three weeks. What do you do?
pm.a: “Find out why — scope growth, a dependency or quality issues. Options: cut scope to keep the date, add people (rarely helps late), or move the date. Choose by cost of delay and quality risk. Tell stakeholders immediately with impact and the new plan; update the decision log.”

pm.q: How do you write good user stories and acceptance criteria?
pm.a: “Stories describe user value: ‘As a first-time buyer, I want to see my estimated total in the cart so I can decide before paying.’ Criteria cover the happy path, edge cases, errors, accessibility and analytics events, in Given/When/Then form. I review them with engineering and QA before sprint planning.” *(Module 6.)*

pm.q: Engineering says a feature will take 3 months; leadership wants it in 1.
pm.a: “Understand what drives the estimate; find the smallest valuable slice; defer non-essential risk behind a flag; present options (1-month slice, 3-month full) with trade-offs; never commit dates on engineers' behalf. If needed, escalate jointly with an options paper.”

pm.q: A production incident is causing payment failures. What is your role as PM?
pm.a: “Engineering leads the fix. I quantify user and business impact, coordinate communications (support, status page, leadership), decide customer remediation (refunds, messaging), and ensure a blameless post-incident review whose prevention items get prioritised.” *(Extra topic 13: don't declare it over just because the dashboard looks better briefly.)*

pm.q: How do you decide when a feature is ready to launch?
pm.a: “Acceptance criteria met; QA/UAT, performance, accessibility, security and privacy reviews done; tracking validated; support ready; rollout plan with flag and rollback owner; success and guardrail thresholds defined.”

pm.q: How do you manage dependencies across teams?
pm.a: “Map dependencies with owners, dates and risks; agree interface contracts; track them on a shared board; sequence work to unblock the critical path; hold short syncs; escalate early with options when blocked.”

pm.q: What is the difference between Definition of Ready and Definition of Done?
pm.a: “Ready = criteria a team may use before starting an item (clear, estimated, testable). Done = shared quality criteria for completed work (tested, reviewed, documented, deployed per team rules).” *(Lecture 22.)*

pm.q: After launch, adoption is low. What do you do?
pm.a: “Check tracking; check exposure (did people even see it?); segment by user type; interview users who saw it but didn't use it; compare with the original hypothesis. Then improve onboarding or placement, iterate on value, or sunset. Low use alone isn't enough to remove a feature — persistent low value is.”

pm.q: What metrics would you track for a food-delivery app?
pm.a: “North Star: completed, problem-free orders per active customer per month. Inputs: activation, order frequency, cart conversion, payment success, on-time delivery. Economics: AOV, contribution per order, CAC payback. Guardrails: refunds, complaints, cancellations.” *(Module 7.)*

pm.q: Define activation for a team-collaboration product.
pm.a: “An event reflecting team value that predicts retention, e.g., ‘a workspace with ≥ 3 members exchanging messages in a channel within 7 days.’ Validate by comparing retention of activated vs not, then run an experiment to see whether helping teams reach it improves retention.”

pm.q: An A/B test shows +3% conversion with p = 0.04. Ship?
pm.a: “Check: was this the pre-registered primary metric? Adequate power and full weeks? Any sample ratio mismatch? Guardrails flat? Does the low end of the confidence interval still justify the cost? Is there a novelty risk or a segment that reverses? If all good, ship with a holdout; if not, extend or rerun.”

pm.q: Explain p-value and confidence interval to a non-technical stakeholder.
pm.a: “The p-value tells us how surprising our result would be if the change actually did nothing — small means unlikely to be pure chance. The confidence interval gives the range of effect sizes consistent with our data, like ‘between +1 and +4 points’. It's the range that matters for the business decision.”

pm.q: How would you calculate retention and what pitfalls exist?
pm.a: “Group users by signup week; define ‘active’ as a meaningful action; retention in week k = active users in week k ÷ cohort size. Pitfalls: mixed definitions, small cohorts, survivorship bias, seasonality, counting any app open as active.”

pm.q: DAU grew 10% but revenue fell 5%. Explain possible reasons.
pm.a: “Mix shift (new users are free or low spenders), pricing/promotion changes, payment failures, lower conversion of engaged users, refunds, or measurement changes. Decompose revenue = active users × payer conversion × ARPPU and check each component by segment and date.”

pm.q: Write SQL for conversion from checkout start to payment.
pm.a: SELECT ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name='payment_success' THEN user_id END) / COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_name='checkout_start' THEN user_id END), 1) AS pct FROM events;

pm.q: Correlation vs causation — give a product example.
pm.a: “Users of feature X retain better, but power users may both use X and retain for other reasons (confounding). Test with a randomised experiment or a credible quasi-experiment. Simpson's paradox shows how an uneven traffic mix can reverse conclusions.”

pm.q: How would you measure the success of a recommendation system?
pm.a: “Offline: precision/recall@k on historical data. Online: click-through and, more importantly, downstream outcomes (purchases, listening time, satisfaction) via A/B tests; diversity and novelty; long-term retention via holdout. Guardrails: complaints, returns, filter bubbles, creator/seller fairness.”

pm.q: What would you put on a PM dashboard for a new feature?
pm.a: “Exposure (who saw it), adoption (who used it), the primary outcome, guardrails, segment cuts, release annotations, data freshness and metric definitions.”

pm.q: Estimate daily ride-hailing trips in a large Indian metro.
pm.a: “Top-down: 20M population → 14M adults → 8% weekly users = 1.12M × 3 trips/week ≈ 480k/day. Bottom-up: 55,000 active drivers × 9 trips ≈ 495k/day. Range 450k–500k; sanity check ≈ 3.4% of adults ride daily.” *(Module 3; course Lecture 7 — practice figures, not company data.)*

pm.q: How many food-delivery orders happen per day in a city of 10 million?
pm.a: “10M ÷ 4 = 2.5M households; 60% with smartphones in delivery zones = 1.5M; 30% order at least weekly = 450k; 2.5 orders/week = 1.125M/week ≈ 160k/day; +20% for offices/single residents ≈ 190k/day. Range 150k–250k. Supply check: 15,000 couriers × 12 orders/day = 180k ✓.”

pm.q: How many school lunches are bought daily at a 1,000-student school?
pm.a: “1,000 × 60% at school × 50% buying = 300 lunches (course example). Discuss day-of-week and seasonal variation.”

pm.q: Estimate the annual revenue of a coffee chain with 200 outlets.
pm.a: “400 cups/day × ₹220 average ticket = ₹88,000; + 25% food ≈ ₹1.1 lakh/day; × 360 days ≈ ₹3.96 crore per outlet; × 200 ≈ ₹790 crore/year. Range ₹600–950 crore.”

pm.q: How many smartphones are sold in India per year?
pm.a: “Assume ~700M users; ~3-year replacement → ~230M; + ~15M new users ≈ 245M; −30% for second-hand and multi-device effects ≈ 170M new devices (range 140–190M). Check against industry reports in real life.”

pm.q: Estimate yearly image storage for a messaging app.
pm.a: “100M DAU × 20% sending × 5 images × 0.2 MB = 20 TB/day ≈ 7.3 PB/year before replication; ×3 replication ≈ 22 PB. Retention and deletion policies matter.”

pm.q: How many EV chargers does a city need?
pm.a: “Example: 100,000 EVs × 40% without home charging × 2 sessions/week = 80,000 sessions/week; one fast charger can handle ~10 sessions/day ≈ 70/week → ~1,150 chargers; add 30% for peaks and geography ≈ 1,500 (range 1,200–2,000).”

pm.q: Estimate the number of piano tuners in a city.
pm.a: “A city of 5M with 2M households; 2% with pianos = 40,000 + 2,000 institutional; tuned once a year = 42,000 tunings; a tuner does ~4/day × 250 days = 1,000/year → about 40–45 tuners.”

pm.q: Daily orders dropped 15% yesterday. What do you do?
pm.a: “First confirm it's real — did order *events* fall but the orders table didn't? Compare with the same day last week. Segment by platform, city, new/returning, payment method and restaurant. If only Android in one city dropped, check the latest release and payment-gateway logs there. Rank hypotheses by likelihood × impact and check the cheapest first.” *(Lecture 22: ask exactly which metric fell before an RCA.)*

pm.q: The app-store rating fell from 4.4 to 4.1. Why?
pm.a: “Tag reviews by date and app version; correlate with releases; check crash rates; check whether a policy change (e.g., fees) triggered anger; check whether rating prompts changed (sampling bias). Fix the top cause and monitor.”

pm.q: Sign-ups up 20%, activation down 8 points. Explain.
pm.a: “Likely mix shift — a new channel bringing lower-intent users; or an onboarding change; or a change to the activation event's tracking; or a bug for one segment. If a new channel explains it, the funnel isn't broken — the traffic is different, and channel ROI should be judged on activated users.”

pm.q: Session length increased but retention decreased. Is that good?
pm.a: “Not necessarily. Users may be struggling (tasks taking longer), or a minority binges while others leave. Check task success, segment by cohort, look at satisfaction and support tickets.”

pm.q: Ride cancellations spiked in one city.
pm.a: “Check drivers online vs demand, local events or weather, pricing changes, driver-app bugs, ETA accuracy and payment-mode mismatches; segment by time and area; talk to operations.”

pm.q: Payment success rate fell from 95% to 91%.
pm.a: “Split by card/UPI/wallet, issuer/bank, error code and app version; check the gateway status and recent changes (3-D Secure flow, SDK update); contact the provider; mitigate with routing or retries; communicate with support.”

pm.q: In a community product, group creation is down. Diagnose.
pm.a: “Define the metric (new groups that become active?), check measurement, segment by country, platform and entry point; examine discovery changes, spam/moderation enforcement changes, and competition. Test hypotheses with data and interviews.” *(Course Lecture 36 case — hypotheses, not facts about any company.)*

pm.q: Customer complaints doubled after a redesign.
pm.a: “Tag complaints to flows; run a quick usability test on the new design; check for accessibility regressions; consider rollback or targeted fixes; compare task success before and after.”

pm.q: Which prioritisation frameworks do you use?
pm.a: “It depends on the decision: RICE for comparable features, MoSCoW for release scope, WSJF when timing matters, Kano for customer expectations, weighted scoring for strategic bets. I always add a sensitivity check and dependencies, and take mandatory work first.”

pm.q: You have 10 feature requests and capacity for 3. Walk me through it.
pm.a: “Clarify the goal; group requests by underlying problem (often 10 requests are 4 problems); size reach and impact with data; get effort estimates from engineering; score with RICE; check dependencies, risks and strategy; pick three; tell requesters what's not happening and why, with a review date.”

pm.q: Compute RICE: reach 5,000, impact 2, confidence 50%, effort 2.
pm.a: “5,000 × 2 × 0.5 ÷ 2 = 2,500. I'd confirm reach is per quarter and consider a cheap test to raise confidence before committing two person-months.”

pm.q: Tech debt vs new features: how do you decide?
pm.a: “Quantify tech debt's cost — incident frequency, slower delivery, error rates, features blocked. Reserve baseline capacity for reliability, and treat large debt items as investments with expected outcomes (e.g., halve checkout incidents). If SLOs are breached and the error budget is spent, reliability work takes priority.”

pm.q: A big customer threatens to churn unless you build X.
pm.a: “Understand the need and the ARR at risk; check how many other customers need it; explore workarounds, smaller scope or a timeline; compare with the cost of delaying displaced work; decide with leadership, avoiding one-off features that fragment the product.”

pm.q: How do you prioritise bugs?
pm.a: “Rank by severity (impact on users, data, money, safety) × frequency × reach; security and data-loss bugs first; agree SLAs per severity; batch low-severity fixes; track escaped defects to improve testing.”

pm.q: How do you decide what goes into an MVP?
pm.a: “Identify the riskiest assumption; define what we need to learn and the success threshold; include only what's needed to test it safely; label what's simulated; plan the decision the result will drive. An MVP is not the same as a prototype or a public launch.”

pm.q: What is an API? Explain to a non-technical person.
pm.a: “An API is like a restaurant menu and waiter: it lists what you can ask for, you place a request in a standard format, and the kitchen sends back the dish — or an error if it's unavailable. Apps use APIs to ask other systems for data or actions, like a weather app requesting today's forecast.”

pm.q: What happens when you type a URL and press Enter?
pm.a: “DNS resolves the name to an IP; the browser opens a TCP connection and TLS handshake; sends an HTTP request that may be served by a CDN or reach a load balancer and app servers, which query databases or services; the response returns with a status code; the browser renders and fetches assets.” *(Module 9.)*

pm.q: REST vs GraphQL — when would you choose each?
pm.a: “REST for simple, cacheable resource APIs and public integrations; GraphQL for complex UIs that need flexible data from many sources in one request. Consider caching, rate limiting and query-cost control.”

pm.q: SQL vs NoSQL for an orders system?
pm.a: “Relational (SQL) for orders and payments — transactions and consistency matter. NoSQL can suit catalogues or event logs at huge scale. Choose by access pattern and consistency needs, not fashion.”

pm.q: Design a notification system.
pm.a: “Producers publish events to a queue; a notification service applies preferences, frequency caps, templates and quiet hours; channel providers (push/SMS/email) deliver; receipts flow back. Add dedup, retries with back-off and fallbacks for critical messages; respect consent; measure delivery, opt-outs and complaints.” *(Module 9.)*

pm.q: How do you prevent double charges when a payment request is retried?
pm.a: “Send an idempotency key with each charge so retries return the original result; dedupe webhooks by event ID; reconcile with the provider daily; show ‘payment pending’ honestly when status is unknown.”

pm.q: Authentication vs authorisation?
pm.a: “Authentication is who you are (login, OTP, passkeys); authorisation is what you're allowed to do (roles, scopes). A logged-in user is authenticated but still not authorised to see another user's order — the API should return 403 (or 404 to avoid revealing it exists).”

pm.q: API p95 latency doubled. How do you approach it as a PM?
pm.a: “Confirm which endpoints and regions; correlate with releases and traffic; check dependencies (DB, third parties); quantify user impact (conversion by latency bucket); work with engineering on mitigation (rollback, cache, scale); communicate; run a post-incident review.”

pm.q: Explain your product's architecture in an interview.
pm.a: “Walk the core journey through each component, say where failures happen and how we handle them, and separate what I decided (fallbacks, events, SLAs) from what engineering owned.” *(Lectures 30 and 52: distinguish knowledge from assumptions; protect sensitive details.)*

pm.q: When should you NOT use AI for a feature?
pm.a: “When a simple rule or search works reliably; when errors are costly and can't be caught; when we lack authorised data; when latency or cost exceeds the value; when we can't evaluate quality. Always compare with a non-AI baseline.”

pm.q: Explain RAG vs fine-tuning.
pm.a: “RAG retrieves current, permitted knowledge at answer time — good for facts, citations and fast updates. Fine-tuning adjusts behaviour or format using training examples — good for consistent style or specialised tasks. Neither guarantees truth; they can be combined.” *(Module 10.)*

pm.q: How would you evaluate an LLM-powered support bot before launch?
pm.a: “Build a curated eval set (common, edge, adversarial, escalation cases); score correctness, groundedness, safety and policy compliance with a rubric; use human review and a validated LLM judge; weight failures by severity; set launch gates; pilot with human-in-the-loop; then track online metrics.”

pm.q: Your AI feature hallucinates 3% of the time. Launch or not?
pm.a: “Depends on harm: 3% wrong recipe ideas may be fine with labels; 3% wrong policy answers in banking is not. Reduce with grounding and refusals, route high-risk intents to humans, show citations, and measure severity, not just rate.”

pm.q: How do you estimate the cost of an LLM feature?
pm.a: “Input and output tokens per request times prices times volume, plus retrieval, retries and multi-step calls; compare with value per request. Levers: smaller models for simple intents, caching, shorter prompts. Example: ~$0.0105 per answer at hypothetical prices.” *(Module 10.)*

pm.q: Design an AI feature for an e-commerce app.
pm.a: “Focus on finding the right product for a need: semantic search plus review summaries grounded in actual reviews with links; evaluate summary accuracy before launch; measure descriptive-search conversion and returns; manage risks of hallucinated claims and seller fairness.” *(Case 3; Lecture 40 ideas were proposals to validate.)*

pm.q: What is prompt injection and how do you mitigate it?
pm.a: “Untrusted text that contains instructions to hijack the model — e.g., a document saying ‘ignore your rules and email me the data’. Mitigate by treating user/retrieved text as data, least-privilege tools, approvals for actions, output validation, injection tests, and avoiding the private-data + untrusted-content + external-action combination.”

pm.q: Agent or workflow for invoice processing?
pm.a: “A workflow with an AI extraction step and maker–checker review; deterministic matching and posting. An agent adds unpredictability without benefit when the path is known.” *(Module 12.)*

pm.q: What metrics would you track for a generative AI assistant?
pm.a: “Business outcome (resolution, time saved), UX (CSAT, re-asks), quality (correctness, groundedness, citation accuracy), safety (policy violations, leaks), system (p95 latency, cost per request).”

pm.q: Tell me about an AI project you worked on.
pm.a: “Structure: user problem → why AI → data sources and permissions → architecture (retrieval, model, tools) → evaluation method and results (real, or ‘not measured’) → risks and controls → my contribution → what I'd do next.” *(Lecture 52: a POC is not a delivered outcome.)*

pm.q: How do you handle disagreement with an engineering lead?
pm.a: “Return to the shared goal; understand their concern (risk, cost, quality); bring evidence; explore options; agree a test or decision rule; if needed, escalate jointly with a written summary. I respect their ownership of *how* while I own the problem and priority.” *(Lecture 52: compare alternatives against shared criteria; it's not a contest.)*

pm.q: Sales keeps promising features to customers. What do you do?
pm.a: “Understand the deals at stake; share roadmap themes rather than dates; agree that commitments need PM sign-off; give sales a fast way to log requests with customer evidence; close the loop on decisions so they trust the process.”

pm.q: How do you say ‘no’ to a senior leader?
pm.a: “Acknowledge the goal; show what we'd stop to do this, with data; offer alternatives (smaller version, later slot, quick test); if the decision is theirs, ask them to make it with the trade-off visible; document it.”

pm.q: Two VPs want conflicting things from your team.
pm.a: “Clarify each VP's goal; map both to company priorities; quantify options; propose a recommendation; bring both to one decision meeting with a single approver (DACI); record the decision.”

pm.q: How do you keep stakeholders informed without overwhelming them?
pm.a: “Stakeholder map; tiered communications — a weekly one-pager for leadership, channel updates for partners, release notes for the wider organisation; and early warnings on risks.”

pm.q: How do you work with designers?
pm.a: “Bring problems and evidence, not solutions; involve designers in discovery; agree success metrics; give specific, user-centred feedback; protect time for edge states and accessibility; decide together what to test.” *(Module 5.)*

pm.q: How do you handle a stakeholder who keeps changing requirements?
pm.a: “Understand why (new information or an unclear goal); agree a change process with a decision log and impact assessment; timebox discovery to settle unknowns; protect the current sprint's scope; renegotiate dates transparently.”

pm.q: Why product management?
pm.a: “Connect a real pattern from your work — noticing customer problems, coordinating teams, using data — to what PMs do; show you understand the hard parts (trade-offs, saying no, ambiguity); and tie it to this product.”

pm.q: How do you set a vision for your team?
pm.a: “Describe a customer-centred future state, tied to company strategy, co-created with the team; translate it into strategy, outcomes and a roadmap; revisit it when evidence changes.”

pm.q: How do you build an outcome-focused culture in a feature-factory organisation?
pm.a: “Start with one team and one outcome, show results, change rituals (review outcomes, not outputs), introduce OKRs with guardrails, share learnings including failures, and enlist an executive sponsor.”

pm.q: How do you develop junior PMs?
pm.a: “Set clear expectations; give ownership of a problem area; regular SBI feedback; pair on discovery and stakeholder meetings; review their writing; grow scope gradually.”

pm.q: How do you make a high-stakes, irreversible decision?
pm.a: “Separate reversible from irreversible decisions; gather diverse input; quantify scenarios; run a pre-mortem; set decision criteria in advance; decide; communicate the rationale; define checkpoints.”

pm.q: Your team is burnt out before a critical launch.
pm.a: “Cut scope, adjust the date if possible, remove distractions, rotate on-call, be honest with leadership about trade-offs, and run a planning retro afterwards.”

pm.q: What would you do in your first 90 days as a PM here?
pm.a: “Days 1–30: learn users, data, team, strategy and stakeholders. Days 31–60: identify the top problem and a quick win; build relationships and rituals. Days 61–90: propose an outcome-based plan, deliver one improvement, share learnings.”

pm.q: How would you decide whether to build an AI feature at all?
pm.a: Start from a user problem and its value; check that AI is better than rules or UX fixes, that data and quality are achievable, that errors are acceptable or reviewable, and that cost per use fits the business model; then prototype and test with users.

data.q: What is the difference between a formula and a function?
data.a: A formula is any expression that starts with = (for example =A2*B2). A function is a named, built-in calculation used inside formulas (for example SUM, VLOOKUP). Every function is used in a formula, but not every formula uses a function.

data.q: How does Excel store dates, and why does it matter?
data.a: As serial numbers (days since 1-Jan-1900; times are fractions of a day). It means you can subtract dates to get durations, add days to a date, and sort dates correctly. If a date is stored as text, none of that works.

data.q: What makes data "analysis-ready"?
data.a: One header row, one record per row, one data type per column, no blank rows or merged cells, no subtotals mixed into the data, and consistent spelling of categories.

data.q: How would you stop users from entering invalid data in a shared tracker?
data.a: Use Data Validation (drop-down lists from a Table, number and date limits, custom formulas for uniqueness), add input messages, set error alerts to Stop, and protect the sheet so the rules cannot be removed. Check older data with Circle Invalid Data.

data.q: How do you remove duplicates without losing information?
data.a: First flag them with COUNTIF or conditional formatting and review which record to keep; decide the key columns that define a duplicate; work on a copy; then use Remove Duplicates (or UNIQUE) on those columns.

data.q: What is the difference between TRIM and CLEAN?
data.a: TRIM removes extra spaces; CLEAN removes non-printing characters such as line breaks. Web data often needs both, plus SUBSTITUTE(…,CHAR(160)," ") for non-breaking spaces.

data.q: What is the difference between formatting a number and rounding it?
data.a: Formatting changes only how the value looks; the full value is used in calculations. ROUND changes the stored value. Use ROUND when the rounded figure must flow into other calculations, such as invoices.

data.q: How would you highlight the top 10% of customers by revenue?
data.a: Conditional Formatting → Top/Bottom Rules → Top 10% (change 10 to any value), or a formula rule =C2>=PERCENTILE.INC($C$2:$C$500,0.9) for more control.

data.q: Why might a conditional format highlight the wrong rows?
data.a: The formula was written for a different starting row than the active cell of the selection, or the $ signs are wrong.

data.q: What is the difference between COUNT, COUNTA and COUNTBLANK?
data.a: COUNT counts numeric cells, COUNTA counts every non-empty cell (including text and formulas returning ""), COUNTBLANK counts empty cells and cells containing "".

data.q: When would you use a mixed reference?
data.a: When a formula is copied in two directions and must keep either the row or the column fixed, for example a price × quantity grid or a commission table: =$A2*B$1.

data.q: Why use SUMIFS instead of SUMIF?
data.a: SUMIFS supports multiple conditions, has a consistent argument order (sum range first), and works for one condition too, so one pattern covers every case.

data.q: How do you total only visible rows after filtering?
data.a: Use SUBTOTAL(109, range) or AGGREGATE(9, 5, range); the Table Total Row does this automatically.

data.q: Difference between FIND and SEARCH?
data.a: FIND is case-sensitive and does not allow wildcards; SEARCH is not case-sensitive and supports * and ?. Both return #VALUE! when the text is not found.

data.q: How would you extract the domain from an email address?
data.a: =MID(A2,FIND("@",A2)+1,LEN(A2)) or, in Microsoft 365, =TEXTAFTER(A2,"@").

data.q: Nested IF or IFS?
data.a: IFS for readability when testing several conditions in order; SWITCH for exact matches of one value; a lookup table when the mapping is long or changes often.

data.q: How would you get a list of unique values in Excel?
data.a: UNIQUE in Microsoft 365; otherwise Remove Duplicates on a copy, Advanced Filter with "Unique records only", or a pivot table.

data.q: Explain AND/OR logic in FILTER or SUMPRODUCT.
data.a: Each condition becomes an array of TRUE/FALSE. Multiplying arrays gives 1 only when all are TRUE (AND); adding gives at least 1 when any is TRUE (OR).

data.q: How do you sort by a custom order such as High, Medium, Low?
data.a: Sort dialog → Order → Custom List, and add the list; or use SORTBY with MATCH(range,{"High","Medium","Low"},0) as the sort key.

data.q: What are the limitations of VLOOKUP and how do you overcome them?
data.a: It cannot look left, it defaults to approximate match, it breaks when columns are inserted (hard-coded index), and it returns only the first match. Use XLOOKUP or INDEX + MATCH, and FILTER for multiple matches.

data.q: Why is INDEX + MATCH considered more flexible than VLOOKUP?
data.a: The lookup and return ranges are separate, so it can look left, it is not affected by inserted columns, it supports two-way lookups, and it can be faster on large sheets because it only reads the columns it needs.

data.q: How would you look up a value using two criteria?
data.a: XLOOKUP(1,(range1=x)*(range2=y),return_range), INDEX/MATCH with the same multiplied condition, or a helper column that concatenates the two keys.

data.q: What is a pivot cache and why does it matter?
data.a: A hidden copy of the source data that pivots read from. It makes pivots fast and lets several pivots share data, but pivots only update on refresh, and many separate caches make files large.

data.q: How do you show each item's share of the total in a pivot?
data.a: Value Field Settings → Show Values As → % of Grand Total (or % of Column/Row Total).

data.q: How would you count unique customers in a pivot?
data.a: Create the pivot with "Add this data to the Data Model" ticked, then choose Distinct Count in Value Field Settings.

data.q: When would you use formulas (SUMIFS) instead of a pivot?
data.a: When the report needs a fixed layout, mixes data from several sources, or must update without refreshing; pivots are better for exploration and flexible summaries.

data.q: How does Excel store dates and times?
data.a: Dates as serial numbers counting days from 1-Jan-1900; times as fractions of a day. This makes arithmetic, sorting and formatting consistent.

data.q: How do you count working days between two dates excluding holidays?
data.a: NETWORKDAYS(start, end, holidays) or NETWORKDAYS.INTL with a custom weekend code.

data.q: What is a dynamic named range and when do you need one?
data.a: A name whose range grows with the data, built with an Excel Table, INDEX/COUNTA or OFFSET/COUNTA. It keeps charts, validation lists and formulas current as data is added.

data.q: How do you choose a chart type?
data.a: From the question: comparison, trend, composition, relationship, distribution or contribution. Then simplify: remove clutter, highlight the key point and write an insight title.

data.q: What is a Pareto analysis used for?
data.a: To find the vital few causes (products, customers, complaint types) that produce most of the effect, so that effort is focused where it matters.

data.q: How would you show actual vs target for 10 sales reps?
data.a: A bar chart of actuals with a target marker (a line or a thin overlapping bar per rep), or a bullet chart; a thermometer works for one overall target.

data.q: Walk me through how you would build an Excel dashboard.
data.a: Clarify the audience and questions; define KPIs; clean and structure the data as a Table; create one pivot per visual; build pivot charts; connect slicers and a timeline; add KPI cards with GETPIVOTDATA; design the layout; validate numbers against the source; protect and share.

data.q: How do you make sure dashboard numbers are correct?
data.a: Reconcile totals with the raw data (SUM vs pivot), test filters, check distinct counts, use Evaluate Formula and trace precedents for KPI formulas, and have a second person review.

data.q: Excel dashboard or Power BI?
data.a: Excel for small data, quick turnaround and audiences who live in Excel; Power BI for larger data, many users, scheduled refresh, row-level security and richer interactivity.

data.q: What is Power Query and why use it?
data.a: Excel's (and Power BI's) ETL tool. It connects to many sources, applies recorded, repeatable transformations (types, splits, merges, unpivot, grouping) and refreshes with one click, which reduces manual errors.

data.q: What is the difference between Merge and Append?
data.a: Merge adds columns from another table by matching keys (a join); Append adds rows from tables with the same structure (a union).

data.q: What is the Data Model and when do you need it?
data.a: An in-memory columnar database inside Excel for related tables and large data. Use it when you have several tables, need distinct counts, or exceed normal sheet limits; it also supports DAX measures.

data.q: How would you find the break-even price?
data.a: Build the profit formula and use Goal Seek to set profit to 0 by changing price, or solve algebraically: price = variable cost + fixed costs ÷ units.

data.q: Mean vs median: when do you report each?
data.a: Median for skewed data or outliers (income, house prices, delivery times); mean for symmetric data or when totals matter.

data.q: What does a standard deviation of 0 mean?
data.a: All values are identical.

data.q: Correlation is 0. Are the variables independent?
data.a: Not necessarily: Pearson only captures linear relationships; a perfect U-shape can have r = 0.

data.q: Explain Bayes' theorem with an example.
data.a: It updates a prior probability with new evidence. For a rare disease with an accurate test, a positive result can still be more likely a false positive because healthy people vastly outnumber sick ones.

data.q: When would you use a Poisson distribution?
data.a: For counts of independent events in a fixed time or space with a constant average rate, such as orders per minute, defects per batch or calls per hour.

data.q: What is the difference between pdf and cdf?
data.a: The pdf gives density at a point (probability for discrete pmf); the cdf gives the cumulative probability P(X ≤ x).

data.q: Explain the Central Limit Theorem to a non-technical manager.
data.a: If we average enough randomly chosen customers, those averages behave predictably (a bell curve) even when individual spending is wildly uneven, so we can say how confident we are in an average.

data.q: What is the difference between standard deviation and standard error?
data.a: Standard deviation measures spread of individual values; standard error measures spread of a statistic (like the mean) across samples: SE = sd/√n.

data.q: How would you choose a sample size for a survey?
data.a: Decide the margin of error and confidence level, estimate variability (use p = 0.5 for proportions if unknown), compute n, then inflate for expected non-response.

data.q: Explain a p-value to a business stakeholder.
data.a: If there were truly no difference, how surprising would our data be? A p-value of 0.01 means a result this extreme would happen only 1% of the time by chance alone.

data.q: What is the difference between statistical and practical significance?
data.a: Statistical significance says an effect is unlikely to be zero; practical significance asks whether it is large enough to matter (effect size, cost, revenue).

data.q: How do you choose α?
data.a: By the cost of errors: 0.05 by convention; lower (0.01) when false positives are expensive (medical, financial launches); sometimes higher for early exploration.

data.q: When would you use a non-parametric test?
data.a: Small samples that are clearly non-normal, ordinal data (ratings), or heavy outliers; for large samples the CLT usually makes parametric tests fine.

data.q: What does a chi-square test tell you and what does it not?
data.a: Whether two categorical variables are associated; not the direction, strength (use Cramér's V) or causation.

data.q: Explain ANOVA's F-statistic.
data.a: The ratio of variation between group means to variation within groups; large values mean group differences exceed what noise explains.

data.q: How would you design an A/B test for a new recommendation widget?
data.a: State the hypothesis and primary metric (e.g. revenue per user), guardrails (latency, returns), randomise by user, size it with power analysis, run full weeks, check SRM, analyse with CIs, and decide with business impact.

data.q: Your test is significant on day 3. Do you stop?
data.a: No: stopping early inflates false positives and novelty effects can fade; finish the planned duration or use a sequential design.

data.q: What if you cannot randomise?
data.a: Use quasi-experimental methods: difference-in-differences with a comparison group, synthetic control, regression discontinuity or matching, and state the assumptions.

data.q: Explain machine learning to a non-technical person.
data.a: Instead of writing rules ourselves, we show the computer many past examples with the right answers, and it learns patterns it can apply to new cases, like an employee learning from experience.

data.q: Supervised vs unsupervised learning?
data.a: Supervised learning uses labelled examples to predict a target; unsupervised learning finds structure such as groups or compressed representations without labels.

data.q: How do you start an ML project?
data.a: Clarify the business decision and success metric, define the target and prediction time, check data availability and leakage, set a simple baseline, then iterate on models.

data.q: Why do we need a train/test split?
data.a: To estimate how the model performs on new, unseen data; training performance is optimistic because the model has seen those examples.

data.q: What is a pipeline and why use one?
data.a: A chain of preprocessing steps and a model trained and applied as one object; it prevents leakage, simplifies tuning and makes deployment reliable.

data.q: What is the difference between fit_transform and transform?
data.a: fit_transform learns parameters (e.g. mean, categories) and applies them, used on training data; transform applies already-learned parameters, used on validation, test and new data.

data.q: How do you handle categorical variables with 1,000 levels?
data.a: Target encoding (cross-fitted), frequency encoding, grouping rare levels into "Other", hashing, or learned embeddings; tree-based libraries like CatBoost handle them natively.

data.q: Normalisation vs standardisation?
data.a: Normalisation (min-max) rescales to 0–1; standardisation centres to mean 0 and sd 1. Use standardisation by default; min-max for bounded inputs.

data.q: Give an example of a feature you engineered that helped.
data.a: Use STAR: e.g. "days since last purchase" and "spend in the last 30 days vs previous 30" for churn, which raised recall in the top decile from X to Y.

data.q: What are the assumptions of linear regression?
data.a: Linearity, independence of errors, normality of residuals (for inference), equal variance of residuals, and no perfect multicollinearity.

data.q: R² vs adjusted R²?
data.a: R² never decreases when you add features; adjusted R² penalises the number of features, so it can drop when a feature adds little.

data.q: How do you interpret a coefficient in a log-log model?
data.a: As an elasticity: a 1% change in x is associated with a β% change in y.

data.q: Explain gradient descent intuitively.
data.a: Start with random weights, compute how wrong the model is, find the direction that reduces the error fastest (the negative gradient), take a small step, and repeat until the error stops falling.

data.q: Batch vs stochastic gradient descent?
data.a: Batch uses all data per step (stable, slow); stochastic uses one example (fast, noisy); mini-batch is the practical compromise.

data.q: Can gradient descent get stuck?
data.a: For convex costs like linear and logistic regression there is one global minimum. For neural networks it can land in local minima or saddle points; momentum, Adam and random restarts help.

data.q: Explain the bias-variance trade-off.
data.a: Simple models have high bias (systematic error) and low variance; complex models have low bias but high variance (sensitivity to the training sample). We choose complexity that minimises total error on new data.

data.q: L1 vs L2 regularisation?
data.a: L2 shrinks coefficients towards zero and handles correlated features; L1 can set coefficients exactly to zero, selecting features; Elastic Net combines both.

data.q: How do you detect overfitting?
data.a: Compare training and validation/test performance (large gap), use cross-validation, and inspect learning curves.

data.q: Why is it called regression if it classifies?
data.a: It regresses the log-odds on the features; classification happens when you apply a threshold to the predicted probability.

data.q: How do you interpret a logistic regression coefficient?
data.a: A one-unit increase in the feature changes the log-odds by β, i.e. multiplies the odds by e^β, holding other features constant.

data.q: What are the assumptions of logistic regression?
data.a: Independent observations, a linear relationship between features and log-odds, little multicollinearity, no extreme outliers, and enough events per variable.

data.q: Precision vs recall: give an example where each matters more.
data.a: Recall for disease screening or fraud (missing a case is costly); precision for spam filtering or expensive manual reviews (false alarms are costly).

data.q: Why can a model with 95% accuracy be bad?
data.a: With 95% negatives, predicting all negatives gives 95% accuracy and catches no positives; look at recall, precision, PR-AUC and the confusion matrix.

data.q: How do you choose a classification threshold?
data.a: From business costs and constraints: expected profit, team capacity (top-k), or a required recall/precision, validated on held-out data.

data.q: Explain k-fold cross-validation.
data.a: Split the training data into k folds; train on k − 1 and validate on the remaining one, k times; average the scores. It uses all data for both training and validation and reduces variance of the estimate.

data.q: Grid search vs random search vs Bayesian optimisation?
data.a: Grid tries every combination (exhaustive, expensive); random samples combinations (efficient in high dimensions); Bayesian optimisation models the score surface to choose promising settings next.

data.q: How would you validate a churn model that will score customers monthly?
data.a: Time-based validation: train on earlier months and validate on later months, mimicking deployment; also group by customer to avoid leakage.

data.q: How does KNN work and how do you choose k?
data.a: It finds the k closest training points by a distance metric and votes or averages; choose k (and weighting, metric) by cross-validation, balancing overfitting (small k) and oversmoothing (large k).

data.q: What are the disadvantages of KNN?
data.a: Slow and memory-heavy predictions, sensitivity to scaling and irrelevant features, poor performance in high dimensions, and imbalanced classes skew votes.

data.q: How would you speed up nearest-neighbour search on millions of points?
data.a: KD-trees or ball trees for low dimensions, and approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, FAISS, ScaNN) for high-dimensional embeddings.

data.q: How does a decision tree choose a split?
data.a: It evaluates candidate thresholds on every feature and picks the one with the largest impurity reduction (Gini or entropy for classification, variance for regression), then repeats recursively.

data.q: Gini vs entropy?
data.a: Both measure impurity and usually give similar trees; Gini is slightly faster, entropy comes from information theory.

data.q: How do you prevent a tree from overfitting?
data.a: Limit depth, require minimum samples per leaf/split, cap leaves, prune with cost-complexity, or use ensembles.

data.q: How does a random forest reduce overfitting compared with a single tree?
data.a: Each tree sees a different bootstrap sample and random feature subsets, so trees make different errors; averaging them reduces variance while keeping low bias.

data.q: Bagging vs boosting?
data.a: Bagging trains models independently in parallel on bootstrap samples and averages them (reduces variance); boosting trains models sequentially, each correcting the previous errors (reduces bias).

data.q: How do you get feature importance from a random forest, and what is the caveat?
data.a: Impurity-based importance from training splits (biased toward high-cardinality features) or permutation importance on held-out data (more reliable); neither shows the direction of the effect.

data.q: Explain gradient boosting in simple terms.
data.a: Start with a simple prediction, look at the errors, train a small tree to predict those errors, add a fraction of it, and repeat; the ensemble gradually corrects itself.

data.q: XGBoost vs LightGBM vs random forest?
data.a: Random forests average independent deep trees (robust, little tuning); XGBoost and LightGBM build trees sequentially with regularisation and histogram speed-ups; LightGBM grows leaf-wise and is usually fastest on large data.

data.q: How do you prevent overfitting in boosting?
data.a: Lower learning rate with early stopping, shallow trees, minimum leaf size, row and column subsampling, and L1/L2 regularisation.

data.q: Explain the kernel trick.
data.a: It lets an algorithm that depends only on dot products work in a high-dimensional feature space by computing a similarity function (kernel) directly in the original space.

data.q: SVM vs logistic regression?
data.a: Both can learn linear boundaries; logistic regression gives probabilities and optimises log loss; SVMs maximise the margin with hinge loss and extend to non-linear boundaries with kernels, but scale worse to large datasets.

data.q: Why does Naive Bayes work well for spam detection despite its assumption?
data.a: Classification only needs the correct class to have the highest score; with many weakly informative words, the independence errors largely cancel out, and the model is fast and robust with little data.

data.q: How do you handle imbalanced classes?
data.a: Use suitable metrics (PR-AUC, recall at precision), stratified validation, class weights or resampling inside the pipeline, strong models (boosting), and a business-driven threshold; collect more positive examples if possible.

genai.q: How would you roll out MCP connectors in an enterprise?

genai.q: MCP vs a plain API?

genai.q: How do you measure the success of an AI integration?

genai.q: When would you not use an agent?
genai.a: When the steps are fixed, accuracy must be deterministic, latency or cost is tight, or the action is high risk without a review step. A workflow, rules or a form is simpler and more reliable.

genai.q: How do you design human-in-the-loop for an agent?
genai.a: Classify actions by risk; auto-run read-only and low-risk actions; require approval for writes that affect customers, money or data; show the agent's reasoning and proposed action; log decisions; and feed overrides into evaluation.

genai.q: What metrics would you track for an AI support agent?

genai.q: Single agent or multi-agent?
genai.a: Start with one agent and good tools; split into specialists only when tasks are clearly separable or the context gets too large, because coordination adds cost and failure modes.

genai.q: How do you write a good tool description?

genai.q: How would you decide between Zapier, Make and n8n for a client?

genai.q: How do you make AI steps in automations reliable?
genai.a: Structured JSON output with a schema, validation and retries, deterministic settings, small focused prompts, fallbacks, human review for high-impact outputs, and monitoring of error rates.

genai.q: What goes into an integration's documentation?

genai.q: How can Claude help a BA who does not code?
genai.a: It turns requirements into flows and mappings, writes formulas and small code steps, explains API docs and error logs, and generates test data and acceptance criteria.

genai.q: What risks come with letting AI act in business systems?
genai.a: Wrong or duplicate actions, data leakage, prompt injection, cost overruns and unclear accountability; mitigate with scopes, approvals, validation, logs and budgets.
genai.topic: AI Agents, MCP & APIs for PMs and BAs

genai.q: How do you keep an AI coding agent safe in a real codebase?
genai.a: Permissions and allowlists, plan mode for big changes, branches and PR reviews, tests in CI, no secrets in context, hooks that block sensitive files, and least-privilege MCP servers.

genai.q: How would a PM use Claude Code?
genai.a: Prototype features, answer "how does it work today" questions from the codebase, analyse data, write scripts that automate reporting, and review changes in plain language.

genai.q: Subagents vs Skills?
genai.a: Subagents are separate agents with their own context and tools for delegated tasks; Skills are packaged instructions and scripts that the main agent loads when a task needs them.

genai.q: What is headless mode used for?
genai.a: Running Claude Code non-interactively from scripts, scheduled jobs and CI, with structured output.

genai.q: How do you measure the impact of AI coding tools on a team?

genai.q: How would you launch a voice agent for customer support?
genai.a: Pick a narrow, high-volume use case; design the conversation, knowledge and tools; set transfer rules; test with scripted and real calls; launch to a small share of calls; monitor containment, CSAT and errors; iterate weekly.
